title: Confirmation
hook: the bishop anoints the forehead with perfumed oil: be sealed with the gift of the Holy Spirit

segments.voice: Yesterday, baptism, water in three names. Your line was your first birthday.

If you've been to a Catholic confirmation, you might remember the smell first. The church is full, teenagers in their best clothes lined up in the aisle, families craning to see. One by one they step up to the bishop, often with a sponsor's hand on their shoulder. He dips his thumb in oil and traces a cross on each forehead. As he gets closer, the front of the church smells faintly sweet, like a perfume counter. That smell has a name: chrism.
screen: `TEENAGERS IN THE AISLE.` → `A THUMB, A CROSS, A FOREHEAD.` → `THE SMELL OF PERFUME.`

segments.voice: Chrism is olive oil mixed with balsam, a fragrant resin. Once a year, usually in Holy Week, each bishop consecrates it at a special Mass, and it goes out to every parish. The word comes from the Greek chrisma, an anointing, the same root as Christ, Christos, the anointed one. In the Bible, kings, priests and prophets were anointed to mark them for a task. In Acts, the people of Samaria hear the Gospel and are baptized. The apostles in Jerusalem send Peter and John, and in the Douay-Rheims, "they laid their hands upon them, and they received the Holy Ghost." Confirmation, Catholics say, continues that moment. As the bishop anoints, he says, in the English form, be sealed with the gift of the Holy Spirit. Sealed, like wax pressed with a signet ring: a mark that says this belongs to someone. The Church teaches confirmation completes baptism and strengthens a person to live the faith in public. Tradition names seven gifts of the Spirit, drawn from Isaiah: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety and fear of the Lord. Eastern churches anoint babies right after baptism and call it chrismation. In the Latin Church it usually comes years later, or for adults at Easter. Many being confirmed also choose a saint's name. It's a custom, not a rule, and in some places it's fading, often because nobody explained it. In the Bible, a new name marks a new task: Abram becomes Abraham, Simon becomes Peter. The point isn't a cool middle name. It's choosing a friend among the saints, someone whose life you'd like to grow into and whose prayers you can ask for. Some keep their baptismal name instead, a sign that confirmation completes baptism.
screen: `OLIVE OIL AND BALSAM.` · `CHRISMA: THE SAME ROOT AS CHRIST.` · `HANDS LAID ON IN SAMARIA.` · `A SAINT'S NAME: A FRIEND FOR THE ROAD.` · then, large: `SEALED.`

segments.voice: The seven gifts again: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, fear of the Lord. Fortitude is courage that lasts, counsel is knowing what to do, piety is a warm love for God; pick the one you need this week. If you pray, ask the Holy Spirit for it by name; if you don't, hold it as a hope, the thing you'd want to be marked with.
Chrism. Olive oil and balsam, blessed by the bishop, from the same Greek root as Christ. Today's word.
Your line: sealed. Marked with the gift of the Spirit, and not alone. Go gently.

howItsDone: In the Latin Church most Catholics are confirmed as young people by the bishop, who anoints their foreheads with chrism; Eastern Catholics and the Orthodox receive chrismation as babies right after baptism.

fork.reveal: Peter and John go down, and "they laid their hands upon them, and they received the Holy Ghost." Catholics see confirmation in that moment.

original.note: Greek: an anointing, or the oil used for it. Christos, the anointed one, comes from the same root.

what a scholar hears: chrisma and Christos share a root; the rite looks back to Acts 8, and East and West give it at different ages.

notes: The confirmation formula 'Be sealed with the Gift of the Holy Spirit' is the ICEL English (copyrighted); used without quotation marks as a description of the words said. Latin: Accipe signaculum doni Spiritus Sancti. Confirm acceptable.
Acts 8:17 DR wording — verify against a Challoner text.
Chrism consecrated at the Chrism Mass, usually Holy Thursday morning or earlier in Holy Week. Confirm.
Seven gifts: from Isaiah 11:2–3 in the Septuagint/Vulgate (piety added). Listed with CCC 1831's names. Confirm.
Confirmation names: a custom, not required. Latin Church age varies by country (US: roughly 7–16). Confirm phrasing.
